Ram Ramirez:
...nicknamed Ram, was born in San Juan, Puerto Rico...
The name was Juan Rogelio Ramirez.
Ah! What was the second one?
Rogelio is Roger.
Oh yes, I see. On the 15th of September, 1913. Now, your mother died when you were three?
Yes. Gabriella Ramirez.
And how did you get to the States?
Well, my (?) relatives and their relatives sent for me and brought me over to the States.
You had a godmother here, did you?
Yeah, I had a godmother here.
You came by ship, of course.
Yes. The ship was the Ponce. I can remember that. That's not necessary, but...
Like Ponce De Leon?
That's right. It was a freighter!
Where did that come to in New York?
Brooklyn. The Puerto Rican Steamship Line. They had a line then.
Do you remember that?
Hosmaden(?), whose father owned the steamship, laundry...no, he owned a laundry company...
Ramirez - 2
In Puerto Rico?
In Puerto Rico.
And when you got here, where did you live then?
On 63rd Street.
You really lived quite a long time there, then.
Yeah. I was raised there. I went to the school, the Henrietta School, which was the Children's Aid Society. They have records there; I have all the records.
You were Catholic, of course.
I went to private Catholic. I was christened at St. Benedict's the Moor right here on 63rd Street. That's how I got my Social Security.
The Moor?
Yes. Moor, like Black. I didn't know how deeply ingrained this Black...! [LAUGHS] Since from the very beginning.
And then you were confirmed by who, did you say, the Bishop...?
Bishop Hayes.
What was he then?
He was a Bishop.
At that time?
Yeah.
When would you be confirmed? When you were about 16?
Ramirez - 3
No, I would say earlier than that.
Oh, earlier.

Like 12. That's not very important, though, you know. In my childhood, I went to the Catholic Church there. And you know, I was part of it. I was confirmed there. And then I stayed in the neighborhood, until then we moved uptown, to Harlem. Well, we moved right to 446 Manhattan Avenue.
Did you get any musical training there?
No, I started with a teacher, you know, who came to the house -- who later I found out didn't have an ear at all! He used to teach the kids. He used to come to their houses and give a 50-cent lesson.
Your grandmother had a piano.
Yeah, we had a piano. And they had a... I would play 'Yes, We Have No Bananas', and I had a little bass... I used to imitate, you know.
Then we moved uptown... I didn't have any formal training then, there... But then I came back and I joined... into the Henrietta School in the community, and met Miss Isabel Stiller.
Where was this?
63rd Street.
And this was the San Juan Hill area.
Ramirez - 4
Yeah. It's still there, and I can take you there -- take a cab and I will show you.
Was that predominantly Black then?

Oh yes. From 60th... It was mixed. From 60th Street, 61st, 62nd, 63rd, 64th is where Procope... Not 65th, which was Irish. It was all surrounded by Irish. That was the reservation. They called it The Jungle. They called it San Juan Hill simply because they used to slide down at that time, you know...
Was it very rough at that time?
Oh yes, very rough.
When you said that they called it The Jungle...

Yes, very rough. But very neighborly. See, they had to stick together because they were surrounded by Irish all around. There were a few Italians, but it was an Irish neighborhood. And that was the time when everything was Irish, because the Irish dominated. Maybe Harlem wasn't Irish, but it may ...(?)... At any rate, it was what you'd call the police chief... It was when Batlin(?) Psyche(?)... You remember Batlin(?) Psyche(?)?
Yes.
He lost his life down here. They killed him down there.
But anyway, in order to cross... We lived in between
Ramirez - 5

Amsterdam...10th and 11th Avenue. If you had to cross the street, boy, you had to fight your way or something to go to...even go to the store. But on the other side of the street you were safe, because you were on your own, you know... And the Italian was the only guy that had the fruit stand, like the Korean is today -- on the corner. The first one I remember... Dominick was the first policeman that... He beat me up and I cried, because I couldn't speak English real good. Setting fires on the street, you know... And I was very scared, and the kids said, "Oh, he's Spanish, he's Spanish."
Can you still speak Spanish?
Oh yeah. I understand it. But I don't think in Spanish, because... I think in English.
But if you don't explain... Well, Mexico...

Oh yeah. It will come back, you know. But I was taught English by English teachers. Campbell, Morrissey. In those days, the teachers were... There were very few Jewish teachers, like they have... They have command of this education today. But then I had Gloria...Miss Campbell... I had all kinds... I had a lot of English...English was taught to me. I remember I had to learn Evangeline in the sixth grade, things like that, you know, and Shakespeare and the whole bit...
Ramirez - 6
Did you do well at school?

Oh yeah. I did pretty well. But we transferred from there to P.S. 7(?) at 116th Street, and then from there to James Fenimore Cooper, which was 184, where Walter Winchell went and Sugar Ray Robinson, you know... So that meant I went from an Irish neighborhood to a Jewish neighborhood. Now, I'm still below 125th Street. The Spanish theatre, the Regent, was at 116th Street. That was the Spanish area...Jewish and a little bit of the Spanish, you know -- they were coming in.

Anybody who was Spanish was Cuban, because then Puerto Rico was not like a place (?). The Spanish theatre was called the Apollo. It was on 125th Street, and it was like a little tiny marquee, and the theatre was in the back. Where the Apollo is now was Hertigan-Seaman's(?). Up there was the Harlem Opera House. Oh, I'll give you a history...
Well, do!

And then the Alhambra, where I saw Florence Mills, was on the Seventh Avenue side. Up above the (?) was the Rose Danceland, not the Roseland Danceland, the Red Rose -- where Johnny Russell played with Billy Cato's band. They used to throw the trombone out in the window. I can remember that.
Billy Cato was a trombone player?
Ramirez - 7
Trombone player.
How big a dance hall was that?
Well, I never... I was too young to know... I could never...
I've heard of it before. But I just... Of course, that was a long time before the Savoy.
It was the Twenties, yeah.
So that would not have been as big as the Savoy.
That was the Twenties. And the Savoy to me was like a... I didn't know anything about that at that time.
When did you start playing...? Oh, you started playing the piano...
Yeah, on the piano... Well, first I played the ukelele.
Oh. Yes?
I was pretty good on the ukelele. We used to do that. Then when I moved uptown... I have a picture of me when I was there. You should see it. I mean, he brought a couple of pictures.

Well, I started playing... I didn't play piano... I didn't get a chance to follow my interest in piano until a kid came on the block playing a little better than I do. I used to play the kazoo, and sometimes I used to play in
little groups, you know. So after that, this guy started to do everything on...taking me all over... Getting my face rubbed and all that! I said, "Oh well" -- I started playing the piano!
So, I remember when I started playing it sounded pretty good, and the rest of the time I... Before I went uptown, I heard Clarence Profit and Bobby Henderson play. That's the next...
Where?

In the YMCA. It was Splicky's(?)... And I played with Jack Snead, a guitar player...he played guitar, man... He was always a cook; he sold hot pies, patties and everything. He used to get me... We used to go... I remember I'd go down to all these studios, and we'd play, you know, in these studios! I never got paid; I got five dollars or something. He took me around, yeah...
Now, you told me once before that one of the first people you heard impress was Earl with Louis -- Earl Hines and Louis Armstrong.
Oh yeah. This is before this.
Oh, this is before!
Yeah!
Well, what was Clarence Profit doing before that?
I don't know. I don't remember
I mean, how well was he playing when you first heard him? He and Bobby Henderson.
Bobby Henderson... They were playing very-very-very clearly(?)... You know, they were playing very well. But when I became around 13, 12...13 or 14, I...
But I understand you were in the union at thirteen.

No, I wasn't in the union yet. But I did a couple of things with Splicky's(?) band, a washboard band, you know -- a couple in Harlem. They were turning around ...(?)... And the union said... By that time the Alhambra had acts, and you were supposed to go on the stage. But when it came time to come on the stage, Splicky(?) himself was saying his man wasn't there, you know...
Who was this Splicky(?)...?
Splicky.
Who was he?
I don't know. He was a washboard player.
Splicky?
Splicky, yeah.
How do you spell that?
That's what we used to call him. I never knew his name.
But he played the washboard anyway.
Yeah. And came time... My guess is he became
Ramirez - 10

a celebrity and I didn't know anything about it!
Now, at this time I went back to the Henrietta School and met Miss Spiller, Isabel Spiller. She is the one that taught me to really read. Before, anything that the teacher would play, I would just play behind with my ear, you know. But she was the first one that taught me to read, and I became interested in playing with the orchestra. Isabel Spiller. Then I went to her school up on 138th Street. She taught at Rodney School, too, I understand, and at the New School -- and she came from New England Conservatory. This woman was... I didn't know then. I mean, I only know recently, when I look in the... Have you got that book, the Negro Professional book, the artist book...?
No.
It's printed in Westport.
Yeah, I've got that.
You've got that?
Yeah.

Well, she's in there! I called Marion Carbon(?) and he told me about it. I said, 'Did you know Miss Spiller?' He said, 'Did I know Miss Spiller?!' -- and he went into it. I didn't know. Here it is. I've got it somewhere...
But she taught you to play piano legitimately.
Ramirez - 11

Legitimately. And with an orchestra, see. And from then on, for another orchestra... She used to have concerts, give concerts at the Lafayette Theatre with amateur musicians, you know. And she taught all over, you know. She was the one that really started opening up my eyes to music, to take piano ...(?)... (?)... to study. "Hold your fingers high." And I used to think, "Why do I have to..." But the old-time piano players were doing all kind of funny things...
Well, the thing was that they were doing all this for show.
Yeah, yeah, for show, see? And I did like Classics.
You didn't.
I did.
Oh, you did.

Yeah, I did. But I never was that interested in it, see. There was a conglomeration of things that happened around that time -- this was about the Twenties, going on the Thirties.

Then of course, I joined the Louisiana Stompers, the Brown Brothers, Louisiana Stompers. We used to play all around...
Well, who were the Louisiana Stompers?
Ramirez - 12
Joe Johnson... The Brown Brothers; it was their band.
The Brown Brothers were saxophone players, right?
Trumpet players.
Trumpet players. Were there two of them?
Yeah. They tried to be like Louis Armstrong.
Who was Joe Johnson?
Joe Johnson was the drummer. Then we had Jordan on trombone. We had U.S. Scott, U.S. "Shorty" Scott on alto. Fats Green...
He was a clarinet player?
Alto player. We were in the same class in junior high school together.
This was in the early Thirties, when you were 17 or 18?
That's right. I might have been 16.
How many men in that band?
We had about nine or ten pieces. Earl McGee on the bass. Leroy Jones on banjo. Sidney Grimes(?) on tenor...
What was his first name?
Sidney. He didn't become a name. Those were the... On the opposite bandstand, when we played the Dunbar Palace, was Horace Henderson Orchestra.
Horace had his own band then.
Ramirez - 13
Yes. We worked up to that as a scrub band, you know.
How long did you play at the Dunbar?
Oh, I think we had a year or two. We went in with Bernie Androtti(?). We played with them all.
We've got to go back a little bit, though, to your own piano style. How was that developing?

Well, it developed to the point when I first heard... At a place called the Cave, on 34th Street and 7th Avenue, I heard Clarence Profit play. He played stride piano. Oh, God, that's the first time I heard piano played like that.
Was he older than you?
Oh yeah.
He was.

He was a cripple. He was a little older. [BORN 26 JUNE 1912] He had trouble with his foot. I don't know what it was. But I know later on he used to have a smell around him, something, you know... And then I heard Bobby Henderson. But Bobby had such big hands that I never thought I'd play like that; you know, his hands were huge. And he played his own style, in octaves. But Clarence Profit really had this (?). He played things like J.P. Johnson, Fats Waller and all those things. Then he was
Ramirez - 14
heard on WHN. I think he played with the Red Devil Stompers; they were a group...
I don't know about them.
Yeah, the Red Devil Stompers.
Was there anybody famous in that band?

No. Well, I'm thinking the piano player who used to play with them...let's see... His name was... Now I forget his name. Arthur... God damn, Arthur, a tall fellow. Gee, if I was to see him again... He really opened up my eyes. Everything about my childhood that I didn't...

Well, anyway, Clarence Profit used to come over as a solo piano, and Arthur Huggins wrote with him. Now, the first song that I wrote was "Baby, Are You Foolin' Me?" and Arthur Huggins did the lyrics and the arrangement on that when I was with the Louisiana Stompers.
What happened to that song?
He's from 63rd Street.
Oh, another one.
Yeah.
Well, I think one thing you haven't said, though, we've jumped over... When we were at 63rd Street, you knew all those people like Benny Carter and Russell Procope.
Oh yeah! And then, Mr. Samuels, Mr. Monk -- they were all there. They were all there! Yes.
Ramirez - 15
Thelonious Monk?

Benny Carter's father was there. I saw Benny Carter's father cut a man's ear from here to here. You know? The guy had hit him, and he came down and he cut that man. But don't say it... I saw him later, a year before he died, and he said, 'Son, how you been?' He didn't even know that I... Because the man, you could see his teeth. And we walked all the way to Russo Hospital here from 63rd Street to (?), hollering at him... And he stayed there the rest of his life, down on 11th Avenue, just hanging out...
Who did? The man or Benny's father?
Benny's father. The man, I don't know what happened to him. I mean, Benny's father. Benny is a tough man, and Benny, don't fool around with him!
No-no, no...
You know that...!
Yeah.

See, I remember it because the band here was in the sewer... Now, we used to play checkers, and use them on the sewer. That's the very sewer where the fight occurred; that's how I remember. Also, Benny used to put me up on a gate, and I couldn't get down. He used to laugh at me... Then Gene Michael, I remember Gene... They were all Byo Scouts, and they used to play, he and Russell Procope...
Ramirez - 16

Russell Procope was the first one I saw play piano. He played "Linger Awhile." That was the closest I saw... That's right. That was a (?). And he had this suit, the Boy Scout suit...and these Scout bands used to play for May parties. They used to go to the Central Park, where they had maypoles -- in the month of May, Maypoles. Every little kid, that was the last (?) of those years.
That tape will be picking up as you go on. We can play it back.
Is this tape recorder on?
Sure it is!
I'll be damned.
You can't talk without recording. Because you know, even some of the things you said, if we did it again, you would forget.

So you learned to play piano early legitimately, and then you were influenced by Clarence Profit. Why did Bobby Henderson go into, like, obscurity? Because nobody heard anything about Bobby Henderson until somebody mentioned records in the Sixties or so. I suppose he worked all that time. Didn't he play in Upstate New York somewhere for a while?
Well, that came afterwards. Now that I know that the recorder is on, I'll try to speak more clearly.
Ramirez - 17

Bobby became involved with my lifestyle at the YMCA. Because when I knew there was an affair... Say, for instance, in Harlem we used to... This is my later years I'm speaking of, you know. When we had a basketball game and dance, after the game there was a dance. You had breakfast dances also, you know, later on in the night that I knew... But it was customary to see a basketball game and dance. And then in my teens, we used to have things like teas. They called them... The college crowd, high school, they weren't not old enough to go to a dance hall; they had these little studios, dance studios or art studios that we had in Harlem. And we had these teas on Sunday afternoon, five o'clock -- or maybe Saturday.
Did you have tea at them?
They called them teas. Well, tea and crumpets.
That was like the Tate(?) Dance Hall.

Well, you can't say cocktails for teeners. You must remember, in those days we had a more strict lifestyle than we have today. Kids weren't allowed to get drunk and go foraging(?) around. So we called them "teas." Maybe one or two will spike it. Don't forget, this is after Prohibition, and the stuff that they sold in those days was horrible, you know. But if you were kind of hip, a hip
Ramirez - 18

teenager, you had a little flask, a little white flask of some of the most volatile stuff that...! So they called it a tea. And therefore, prior to playing for a social house or rent parties, you played in these teas -- I mean, for five dollars. That's a lot of money.

You asked me what made me go into playing piano, to be a musician. It was better than working in a grocery store, or delivering suits at a tailor, a place... Like, we had the Spotless Cleaners and the Burger Service and things like that, you know. I done that also. Then I found that it was more to my liking. Then back in my teens I also had jobs at a furrier. Of course, even in the summertime, I tried that, when there's no school... The only thing about it, like, the boss was say, "Roger, on your way home drop these packages off." I wouldn't get home until 7 o'clock that night! And then I can remember going into the cold storage in the summertime; you'd have to put on an overcoat in there!

Anyhow, playing piano was a little more so to my liking as a livelihood, you know. So I got to make some extra money. And then I saw everybody was doing that. I met fellows playing violin, the saxophone...
Where was this?
Well, this was in different places in Harlem. One place called the Cave. We had the Black and Gold
Ramirez - 19

Studio, the Jack and Jill Studios. Different places where the youngsters used to meet. And therefore, there was always a piano player, and then everybody that played piano would be around. "Well, So-and-So is going to be here, he's going to play," and "So-and-so is going to play here." And then there would be piano battles.
What date do you think we're talking about now?
Mmm, this is around the early Thirties.
The Louisiana Stompers are the early Thirties...
Well, it could happen at the same time.
Oh yes, yes.

Because, you know, Dunbar Palace we'd play on weekends, maybe a day, or maybe a dance... They had many social clubs in those days. And at the Renaissance, I mean, you had... Vernon always had a dancing band. He had Metcalf, he had Roy Eldridge...
What sort of music did the Louisiana Stompers play?
We played Jazz, you know...
Yeah, but did you have arrangements or...?
Oh, we had arrangements.
So it wasn't sort of Dixieland type. I suppose you played stocks?
Yeah. Well, we played things that... We had managed to get arrangements from Benny Carter, and we traded
Ramirez - 20

in those years, you know. Then we played "Chinatown". We used to buy them from the guy that... There were covers... And the big bands were selling them to the other bands. That was the big thing in those days. Then I had made a few. As soon as I learned to read... Boy, I read a book by Frank Scranton(?), and I began to orchestrate immediately! I'll never forget when I (?) read.

So along in the pursuit of studying, I studied a bit with Kincaid, harmony... Then I had a... Who else? I had a teacher who... Gee, I forget the guy's name. Then of course, I had... At Commerce High School, we... I was in the band in the school; my instrument was a bassoon, believe it or not. It was a symphony orchestra. I didn't do too well there; I can tell you that. Because they ran out of instruments! And piano wasn't required there at the time; you know, glockenspiel. I didn't... Actually, I played also some piano. I stayed there...
I don't want to skip too much. So much happened in those years...
Well, try and remember everything. How long do you continue to write arrangements?
Well, I didn't write too much. Not too much. I left the band... When I left the band I went to Rex Stewart.
Ramirez - 21
The books mention a cat named Monette Moore.
Oh, well... It's good you're bringing memories back, you know. There was a circuit at night in the various bar-and-grills; it would be a singer and vocalist.
Pardon?

Singer and vocalist. Every bar-and-grill had a back room where people sat down, and you had a piano player and a singer. So Monette Moore was in one of these... I forget... Was it the Alhambra? There were so many of them up in Harlem. And they were very popular, and they all had, you know, their own style of singing. I started playing, and I liked the way she sang...
She was quite popular at that time, too, wasn't she?
Yes, she was. She was.
She used to sort of growl, as I remember.

Yeah. And I didn't even know how popular she was until a young fellow named John Hammond came from Yale down there, and used to sit... Heh-heh! He was very enthusiastic. And then, of course, he shed a lot of light as far as Jazz and singers were concerned to me at that time. Because I didn't think all this stuff was so popular!
The accompanying was good for you, wasn't it.
Yes.
Because you have to play a lot of different songs.
Ramirez - 22

Right! Now, we're still in the Thirties. Remember, there was an old vocalist by the name of Bessie Smith. She was pretty fair/fat(?). And we had an elderly Jewish gentleman in there, you know...until I found out he was her husband! But I remember her.
He was a sort of agent, I take it.

An agent. The house was on 153rd Street, and it's still there. I always remember it, you know. She lived upstairs. She had been a singer at one time, she told me. Today I know who it was, but then I didn't know. And then there was a popular...
[END OF TAPE 1, SIDE 1]
You were talking about Bessie Smith.

So he asked me if I want to go play with her. And God knows, I didn't know where she was singing, I didn't know where I was playing... I took a few drinks; it was awful. Anyhow, I went with her to Binghamton, New York, at a theatre. I remember we stayed in a little house... Johnson City and Binghamton were together. And it's unbelievable to me that I can say I once played for Bessie Smith. It was a very unhappy situation, because you know, I was very inexperienced. And it only lasted I think about a
Ramirez - 23
weekend or so.
Was she tough with you?
No, she just said that I had...
But you say you were very inexperienced. But you could play enough for her.

Yeah, I played enough for her. And then we did a broadcast there. But to me it was a terrible place to be in. It seemed to me like it took years to get up there. In those days the bus...we went by bus, you know. And that was a pretty long trip.
How far would it be actually?
From here to Binghamton? Oh my goodness... Today, by our standards, not too far. It's just a jump of several hours, about four or five hours.
Oh, it was quite long.
Yeah, it was. But the buses in those days, you know, made a lot of stops. Then I got back; I don't know how I got back, but I did. But I still played with the band, you know.
Was this before you played with Monette Moore or afterwards?
Well, I would say around the same time. You must remember in New York City a lot of things happened. People usually say, 'Well, I came from a small town, I did
Ramirez - 24

this in a small town." But here in New York, to me, this is... Everything is happening from... You know, you get the realization then as a kid... I'm playing with kids for a month, a year, and then next thing...it just changes; it's a constant change of (?) around.
Well, look, we're talking of fifty years ago.
Right now... Oh, my God...
So I mean, naturally a lot of things jumble.
It is. I mean, to me, like fifty years ago...
But after the Louisiana Stompers... Now, you figure that went on for about two years, huh?
I would say so.
And then you joined Rex Stewart at the Empire Ballroom. Now, this is the summer of '33. Would that be right?
That sounds right.
And how did Rex know about you?

I don't know. That's a good question. I do know... U.S. Scott. He was an alto player, a good buddy of mine, we went to school together. Possibly he was the one who recommended me. Maybe that's... I just don't remember how it...
Well, maybe Rex was in that Horace Henderson band that played opposite you.
No, he wasn't.
Ramirez - 25
He wasn't?
Sandy Williams was.
Oh, was he?!
Sandy Williams... I can remember. Jack Butler, Bob Carroll. Manzie Johnson on drums. Rupert Coles, Honi Coles' father. Quinton Harrington...
I don't know him. What did he play?
Alto.
Who were the trumpet players?
Jack Butler, Gus MacLellan(?). Sandy Williams. It was a ten-piece band.
Were they up at Dunbar a long time, too?
Yeah, he was the house band.
Oh, they were.
They were. And we were the second band.
Well, that was a pretty good gig.
Yeah. And then Chu Berry joined them after that. He had an influx of musicians, Horace Henderson did - - he had a good band.
Horace must have been... Horace always seemed to have had a rather bad fate. But he must have been pretty knowledgeable in his own right to have got musicians like that.
Well, he was Fletcher Henderson's brother!
Ramirez - 26
But everybody rather sort of claims to think he wasn't much good.
I understood he came from Wilberforce Music School.
Yeah, he did. But in later years he wrote good arrangements, and he was a nice piano player.

Well, (?) was self-taught to a degree. My education in music came further along the line, after I fished around a lot, you know. Then later on, when I began making a conscious effort into my music...or attention, you know...
Well, it seems to me in that period the fact that so many people were largely self-taught was not such a bad thing as it may seem, because it resulted in a lot of individuality. Didn't it?

Well, yeah... Well, I would say Jazz primarily... I mean, my attention to Jazz, I was right in the midst of it. So whatever, no matter what it was, I had to play some of it somehow. When I should have been playing in the church more often, I played at night, you know. I stayed away from school a lot, you know. And I heard all the piano players who came to New York eventually. I would be right up there, you know, losing sleep listening to them. And a lot of them came here to Gotham, in New York, and stay
Ramirez - 27
here. And they'd come from all over -- from the Mississippi, from Kansas... Look at it. This is the mecca. And I just learned(?) the mecca, trying to get that thing, you know.
Well, by 1933, you had heard the people like Fats and James P. and Earl...

See, I go back early, because this is my early childhood... I always go to that...my first realization of it. I remember Fats Waller, the first time I saw him, I saw the back of him -- I saw this fat guy. And I heard it from everybody: 'Have you ever heard Fats Waller?' Well, I'm playing ball then, you know. 'Oh yeah...' One time... I'd heard so much about him and his piano playing. One day they mentioned Fats Waller... He was at some kind of special show. I saw him playing... I was really far from the keys. But I saw the back of him. And he just sauntered on the stage and played. At this time, all the time, he was playing the organ at the Lafayette Theatre, sing-alongs and different things...
You mean when they had the bouncing ball on the screen?
